comments.author: BenefitGrand8752
comments.body:
Yes, I built one, though I’m not quite the case you’re asking about: I’m not a professional, but I’ve been trading for 8 years.

The bot works: it’s been running live on my eToro account for about two weeks. It watches the market, applies my rules, places the orders and logs everything. An AI coding assistant wrote most of the code, but the rules come from my own experience.

“Working” and “profitable” are two different things, though, and two weeks tells me nothing about the second one. What I’ve learned so far:

* AI builds the software, not the edge. It will happily automate whatever strategy you describe, including a losing one.
* Costs kill most ideas. Lots of strategies look great in a backtest and disappear once you add spreads and fees.
* Most of the work is safety, not strategy. Position limits, stop losses, what happens if the connection drops mid-order.
* Start without real money. I ran it in shadow mode (decisions logged, no orders) before going live, and then only with small amounts.

So, to your actual question: I don’t think it works with zero trading knowledge. The AI can write the bot, but someone has to tell it what to do and judge whether the results make sense, and that’s where my 8 years went. Without that, a bot just executes bad decisions faster and without sleeping. Learn the basics first, and be very skeptical of anyone selling a “profitable bot”: if it really worked, they wouldn’t be selling it.

Btw, should you be curious about what I've written, have a look to this introdution (the look is similar to etoro as I have 3 different templates fot the current UI)
https://youtu.be/H1KLmyQso3o

replies.author: Kilo3407
replies.body: How do you find your edge? Any books, info, methodologies that you can recommend? Thanks

replies.author: BenefitGrand8752
replies.body:
For “edge” I understand a statistical advantage: something in your rules that, over many trades, makes you more than you lose. Two things make it hard to find. Costs eat it easily: a spread or a fee can turn a small advantage into a loss. And the classic trap is believing you have one when you don’t. Many backtests show an edge that is really just the strategy fitted to past data.

My approach, and it’s just mine, is to run both a backtest and a forward test. For the forward test I use what I call shadow mode: the strategy runs on live market data and logs every decision it would make, but places no real orders. It’s the most honest test, because the strategy is facing data it has never seen. I also test many strategies in parallel, and the forward test is what shows me which good backtests were just luck.

What I’ve seen, at least on eToro, is that with retail transaction costs short-term strategies like scalping or intraday trading don’t pay off. You trade too often and the costs swallow whatever you gain. Medium and long-term strategies, holding for weeks or months, work much better because each trade’s cost is small compared to the move you’re aiming for. If you could get costs really low, with a broker that has tight spreads and low commissions, some short-term approaches would start to make sense. Two examples are intraday mean reversion (betting that a sharp move partly reverses) and pairs trading (buying one stock and shorting a closely related one when their prices drift apart).

comments.author: eduard_trades
comments.body:
Yes, and it's the right order. Several exchanges have demo or testnet accounts with the same API as real trading: Bybit has demo trading, Binance has a futures testnet, Hyperliquid has a testnet. Your bot talks to them exactly as it would to a real account, only with fake money.



What I'd do:

1. Write your rules in plain words first: when to enter, where the stop goes, how much to risk per trade. If you can't write them down, a bot can't follow them.

2. Let the bot only log what it would do for a couple of weeks, without placing orders.

3. Then run it on the demo account and compare its fills with the prices it expected. That gap is your real cost.

4. Only then small real money.



One warning: a demo fills you more nicely than a real market does, so treat a small demo profit as roughly zero.

comments.author: qzy4628
comments.body: Deffo begin with basics of trading, a good foundation will help you understand what direction the bot must go in. I don’t mean buy or sell but what flaws need fixing, what needs considering and proper RR. I started building a forex trading bot and developed that for a few months till it was profitable, i then got really big into validating and edge finding and eventually shattered my entire system due to the results of an in depth backtest. Forex is incredibly hard to build a bot for and the results showed my “Profitability was luck and rules” I ran more tests and moved to NQ futures and since it’s been up. It jusg passed its first funded account and many more to come. Don’t be discouraged by negative results, when searching for an edge or strategy more often that not you will be returned nothing, it doesn’t exist. Think about how you structure the research and what possible bases to cover then validate out of sample, forward test and validate to your system.
